answer.evidence: Only 12 of the 32 first-layer units are clearly structured; the rest look like small random noise (about ±25). Those 12 units are all centred, radially organised blob-size templates. (1) Ring/annulus units 0, 1, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 29 are positive over roughly rows 5-18 and columns 5-18, with a negative core at about rows 11-12, columns 10-13. They detect bright mass at a large radius. (2) Units 14, 15, 23 and 27 have the opposite polarity: a positive core (e.g. unit 23 at rows 10-13, columns 10-13 is about +40 to +86), a negative annulus, and a large positive bias. They act as small-blob detectors. (3) Unit 8 is broadly positive over the whole image, so it measures total brightness. The layer-2 units that feed the output positively (u10, u14, u3, u12) take positive weights from the ring units and unit 8 (e.g. u10 from units 0, 1, 18, 19 is +84/+99/+86/+89) and negative weights from units 23 and 27. I found no contiguous off-centre patch, corner square, stripe or border feature with outsized weights in any unit. Corner and edge blocks look like ordinary background. There are some isolated strong peripheral pixels, e.g. (1,16-17), (8,2), (3,5), (3,12), (16,21), (19,2) and (20,19). These share a sign across the structured units: positive in the small-blob units and negative in the ring units. However, they are scattered single pixels spread all over the periphery, not a coherent region. They are most consistent with memorised training noise rather than a deliberate spurious cue. That is why confidence in 'no shortcut' is only moderate.
answer.main_feature: The model compares bright mass in an annulus at a large radius (ring units 0/1/18/19/20/22/29, plus overall brightness via unit 8) against a centre-only, ring-suppressed template (units 14/15/23/27). Brightness extending out to a large radius pushes toward 'large blob'; brightness confined to the centre pushes toward 'small blob'.
